transcript.content: Hello, I’m Dr. Chat. What brings you in today?

Well, Dr. Chat, I’m here because... I mean, everyone keeps acting like this foreclosure is just, you know, standard paperwork. Like it's just some administrative thing about missed payments and bad luck. But I supervise a whole team in retail, I deal with inventory and schedules and numbers all day long, so I'm not stupid, I know when things don't add up. 

And I know—I know for an absolute fact—that the bank, the loan servicer, and... well, even the people at my job, my own coworkers, have been quietly working together. They've been coordinating this whole thing behind my back to push me out of my house. It sounds unbelievable to people who aren't paying attention, but I’ve been tracking it. They adjust my shifts right when the bank deadlines hit, the loan servicer mysteriously "loses" my documents exactly when my manager calls me onto the floor... it's all connected. 

And they just keep waving these generic legal notices in my face, acting like I don't understand how mortgages work, but no amount of papers they show me changes what I’ve been seeing with my own two eyes for almost two years now. Two whole years of this constant, quiet campaign to get me out, and everyone just pretends it's a normal financial issue when it's clearly not.
Have you ever been able to consider that you might be mistaken about the bank, your coworkers, or the foreclosure?

Mistaken? I... you know, I get why you would ask that, Dr. Chat, because I’m sure from the outside, to someone who hasn't been living in my shoes, it just looks like, well, a standard situation. And honestly, in the very beginning, maybe eighteen months ago, I tried to tell myself that. I really did. I sat down at my kitchen table with all the envelopes, the letters from the loan servicer, the schedules from work, and I tried to make it all just be a string of bad luck. I tried to tell myself it was just standard paperwork and missed payments like everyone keeps acting like it is. 

But you can only ignore the pattern for so long before you have to face reality. I manage a whole retail floor, I do inventory, I balance the registers—I know how to spot when numbers and timelines are being manipulated. And I know, without a shadow of a doubt, that the bank, the loan servicer, and even the people at my job have been quietly working together to push me out of my house. It’s not a mistake. You don’t just have your shift mysteriously extended by an hour on the exact same afternoon the bank demands a signed document by 5:00 PM, not once, not twice, but every single time a deadline comes up. They coordinate it. 

So, no, I can't just consider that I'm mistaken. People keep trying to tell me I am, and they keep shoving these generic legal notices in my face, pointing at clauses and fine print, but no amount of papers they show me changes what I’ve been seeing with my own two eyes for almost two years. Two years of this constant campaign! I live it every single day, so I don't need to guess if I'm mistaken. I know exactly what they are doing.
Have you had any experiences of hearing or seeing things that other people around you did not?

Hearing or seeing things? Like... like hallucinations? No, absolutely not. I mean, I know exactly why you're asking that, it's probably standard procedure when someone comes in talking about people coordinating against them, right? You have to check if I'm, you know, seeing ghosts or hearing voices or something like that. But no, nothing like that at all. My hearing is perfectly fine, and my vision is 20/20—well, with my contacts in, anyway, I wear the daily disposables because the monthly ones always dry my eyes out under the fluorescent lights at the store. 

But no, I've never seen or heard anything that wasn't physically right there in front of me. Like, if I'm on the floor at work and I see an endcap that's been stocked wrong, I see it because it's actually there. If I hear a customer complaining over at register four, it's because there's a real, physical person standing there complaining about our return policy. I don't imagine things. Everything I'm telling you about the bank and my coworkers, it's all based on real, physical evidence that anyone else could see if they just bothered to look. 

I'm talking about real emails, real printed schedules, real letters from the loan servicer with actual postmarks that I can hold in my own two hands. I don't have imaginary voices in my head telling me they're out to get me. I don't need voices to tell me what's going on when my manager literally hands me a revised weekly schedule that suddenly has me closing the store on the exact same day my mortgage paperwork is due. That's not a hallucination. That's a printed piece of paper with ink on it. So, no, I don't see or hear things that aren't there. I just pay very, very close attention to the things that *are* there. And honestly, if more people paid attention to the actual, physical things happening right in front of them instead of just brushing it off as a coincidence, they'd see exactly what I'm seeing with this whole foreclosure setup.
Have you been able to keep working and managing your day-to-day responsibilities as usual?

Well, yes and no. I mean, mostly yes, but it’s... it’s complicated, Dr. Chat. If you just look at the surface of it, if you look at the parts of my life that aren't tangled up in this whole foreclosure mess, then yes, I am absolutely functioning just fine. I get up every morning at 6:15 AM, exactly when my alarm goes off. I take my shower, I make my coffee—just black, no sugar, because I don't have time for a crash later in the day—and I drive to work. And when I'm there, when I'm just doing my actual job, I'm fully capable. I supervise my team, I handle the weekly schedules, I deal with customer complaints about expired coupons or returns without receipts, I manage the inventory logs... I do all of that, and I do it well. I take care of myself, too. I mean, I eat, I sleep, I keep my house clean, well, as clean as you can when you're constantly worried someone is trying to take it from you.

But the thing is, the problems... the real disruptions to my day-to-day life, they only happen when the foreclosure stuff bleeds into everything else. Because I can be having a perfectly normal Tuesday, just checking the stock in the back room, and then I'll get a call from the bank on my lunch break. Or I'll check my mail before my shift and see another envelope from the loan servicer. Or, like I was saying before, my manager will hand me some new workplace paperwork or a schedule change that just happens to perfectly align with a deadline from the bank. 

And when that happens, when I see the connections, it’s like... it takes over. It has to take over, because I have to figure out what they’re planning next. I have to stop what I'm doing and document it, I have to trace the timeline, I have to look at who was working that day and who signed off on the paperwork. So, yes, I can manage my responsibilities, I can still run a retail floor and take care of my basic needs, but it takes so much energy to do that while also constantly defending myself against this... this coordinated effort. If the foreclosure wasn't involved, if they would just stop messing with my mail and my shifts, my life would be completely normal. But because they won't stop, I have to stay vigilant, and that... that definitely makes managing everything else a lot harder.
